title: The Pipe Under the Bow
topic_used: Bearspaw South Feeder Main: 2024 and 2025 breaks, Independent Review Panel finding that the risk was identified after the 2004 McKnight failure and inspections designated 2017/2020/2022 did not occur, and the new steel pipe (microtunnelled under the Bow) being connected under Stage 4 from Nov 4, 2026

title: Calgary's 2027 budget: what the preliminary numbers say
topic_used: Preliminary 2027–2030 budget figures Council released Sept 29, 2026 (C2026-0749 Rev. title: Who was Deerfoot? The runner behind Deerfoot Trail
topic_used: Deerfoot (Api-kai-ees), Siksika (Blackfoot) runner and nephew of head chief Crowfoot: autumn 1886 ten-mile race in Calgary, beat J. W. Stokes of Birmingham by a full lap; miscount claim, race rerun; entered after Stokes had run six laps and still passed him, finishing in 54:30; Deerfoot Trail named in his memory in the 1970s (DCB)
central_figure: In the autumn 1886 ten-mile race in Calgary, Deerfoot beat J. W. Stokes by a full lap; in the rerun he entered after Stokes had completed six laps and still passed him (Dictionary of Canadian Biography, 'Api-kai-ees')

title: The Georgia town behind Calgary's Field of Crosses
topic_used: Field of Crosses origin: Calgary businessman Murray McCann saw roadside crosses honouring the fallen in Menlo, Georgia, took the idea to the Calgary Poppy Fund; a few hundred crosses on Memorial Drive in 2009 (VAC 500; board chair 300), more than 3,700 in 2026, honouring thousands of southern Albertans who died defending Canada
central_figure: More than 3,700 crosses in 2026 (Global News, Nov 4, 2026), from a few hundred in 2009

title: Three Places, One Military Story
topic_used: Remembrance Day story in three places: Mewata Armoury (1917-1918 Tudor Gothic drill hall; per Parks Canada completed too late to be of practical value in WWI; HQ for all Calgary militia units 1918-1939; WWII training camp; National Historic Site 1989), Currie Barracks (land acquired 1933, named for Gen. Sir Arthur Currie; Depression relief project; Queen Elizabeth II stayed overnight in the Officers' Mess; decommissioned 1997; now the Currie neighbourhood, Provincial Historic Resource 1999), The Military Museums (Sir Sam Steele Junior High made surplus, Calgarians raised $6.5M; opened by Queen Elizabeth II as the Museum of the Regiments in 1990; renamed 2006)
central_figure: Mewata Armoury was 'completed too late to be of practical value during World War I' (Parks Canada, Directory of Federal Heritage Designations), then served as headquarters for all Calgary militia units 1918-1939

title: Who was Crowchild? The chief behind Crowchild Trail
topic_used: Crowchild Trail is named after David Crowchild, chief of the Tsuut'ina Nation 1946-1953; he gave his blessing to the road name after city officials asked his permission (The Sprawl), and said 'May this be a symbol of cutting all barriers between all peoples for all times to come' (Alberta Champions; Imagine/mycalgary.com). Naming year not used (sources say 1966 / 1968 ribbon / 1971).
central_figure: David Crowchild, chief of the Tsuut'ina Nation 1946-1953 (Calgary Guardian; Avenue Calgary); gave his blessing when city officials asked to name the road after him (The Sprawl)

title: Calgary cloned a war memorial
topic_used: Memorial Drive's memorial poplars: first tree planted by Mayor Adams in 1922 on Sunnyside Boulevard (now Memorial Drive); the plan was a tree for each fallen soldier of the Great War; in 2001 the City harvested live cuttings from the remaining trees and grew cloned memorial trees at a tree farm in Grand Forks, B.C., so the memorial poplars can be replaced (City of Calgary; Veterans Affairs Canada). Tree counts and the exact day left out because the sources differ.
changed_from_calendar: Kept the calendar topic, sharpened to its most surprising part (the clones).
